# Digest R3 — James 2:14–26 (faith, works, justification)

**Source:** Douglas J. Moo, *The Letter of James* (PNTC, 2000)  
**Cache:** `R3-2_14-26.txt` (raw L932–1093)  
**Scope:** James 2:14–26 — the theological climax of the letter  
**Extractor role:** digests only; no wiki edits; no task-observer  
**Attribution:** all claims are Moo’s unless marked as Moo citing another (Luther, Calvin, Jewish tradition, etc.)

---

## Claims

### C-R3-001 — Unit is the letter’s most theologically significant and controversial paragraph
**Claim:** Moo holds that James 2:14–26 is the most theologically significant and most controversial unit in the Letter of James; taking the right approach to the unit as a whole is therefore critical before detailed exegesis.  
**Quote:** “This paragraph is the most theologically significant, as well as the most controversial, in the Letter of James.”  
**Locus:** R3 L1; James 2:14–26 intro

### C-R3-002 — Moo’s structural outline of 2:14–26
**Claim:** Moo outlines the passage as: Introduction (v. 14, “What good is it?”) → A. Illustration (vv. 15–16, same question) → Conclusion: faith by itself without action is dead (v. 17) → B. Objector: faith and deeds are separable (v. 18a) → James’s responses and OT examples, with v. 24 as the center.  
**Quote:** “Introduction of topic: faith without works cannot ‘save’ (v. 14) (What good is it?) … A. Illustration (vv. 15-16) … Conclusion: faith by itself, if it is not accompanied by action, is dead (v. 17) … B. An objector: faith and deeds are separable (v. 18a)”  
**Locus:** R3 L5–11; Jas 2:14–18a

### C-R3-003 — Concentric / ring structure with v. 24 at the center
**Claim:** On Moo’s reading, after the objector, James’s first response is practical (only deeds demonstrate faith, vv. 18b–19); the second opens with “You foolish man,” framed by an inclusio “faith without works is useless/dead” (vv. 20 and 26); Abraham and Rahab occupy the next ring (vv. 21–23, 25); the center is the plural address of v. 24.  
**Quote:** “James makes the point of this response clear by beginning and ending with the same emphasis (an inclusio): ‘faith without works is useless/dead’ (vv. 20 and 26). The examples of Abraham and Rahab occupy the next inner ‘ring’ of the argument (vv. 21-23 and 25), while the center of the structure is highlighted with another direct address of the readers: ‘You [plural] see that a person is justified by what he does and not by faith alone’ (v. 24).”  
**Locus:** R3 L14–15; Jas 2:18–26

### C-R3-004 — Theme thrice announced: dead / useless faith without works
**Claim:** Moo says James leaves no doubt about the theme, announced three times: faith by itself without action is dead (v. 17); faith without deeds is useless (v. 20); faith without deeds is dead (v. 26).  
**Quote:** “James leaves us in no doubt about the theme of this paragraph, announced three separate times in the course of the argument: • faith by itself, if it is not accompanied by action, is dead (v. 17) • faith without deeds is useless (v. 20) • faith without deeds is dead (v. 26)”  
**Locus:** R3 L17–23; Jas 2:17, 20, 26

### C-R3-005 — “Dead” faith fails its purpose: it cannot save or justify
**Claim:** For Moo, such faith is “dead” in that it does not attain its purpose: it cannot save (v. 14) or justify (v. 24).  
**Quote:** “In what way is such faith ‘dead’? In the sense that it does not attain its purpose: it cannot save (v. 14) or justify (v. 24).”  
**Locus:** R3 L24; Jas 2:14, 24

### C-R3-006 — Not works added to faith, but genuine faith characterized by works
**Claim:** Moo insists James is not arguing that works must be *added* to faith; rather, genuine biblical faith will inevitably be characterized by works. Adding works to a bogus faith is futile.  
**Quote:** “James is not arguing that works must be added to faith. His point, rather, is that genuine biblical faith will inevitably be characterized by works. Trying to add works to a bogus faith is an exercise in futility”  
**Locus:** R3 L24; Jas 2:14–26 synthesis

### C-R3-007 — Only implanted-word transformation produces works pleasing to God
**Claim:** Moo monergistically ties true works to prior grace: only by “accepting the implanted word” (1:21) and the inner transformation it brings can one produce works pleasing to God.  
**Quote:** “for only by ‘accepting the implanted word’ (1:21) and experiencing the inner transformation that it brings can one produce works pleasing to God.”  
**Locus:** R3 L24; cross-ref Jas 1:21; 2:14–26

### C-R3-008 — Deeds of obedience as a “test” of genuine faith
**Claim:** Moo frames 2:14–26 as proposing a “test” of the genuineness of faith: deeds of obedience to the will of God.  
**Quote:** “James, in a sense, proposes for us in these verses a ‘test’ by which we determine the genuineness of faith: deeds of obedience to the will of God.”  
**Locus:** R3 L24–25; Jas 2:14–26

### C-R3-009 — Immediate context: judgment under the law of liberty (2:12–13)
**Claim:** Moo links 2:14–26 first to 2:12–13: the warning of judgment according to the “law of liberty” raises the question what kind of faith provides security in the judgment.  
**Quote:** “James’s warning that believers will be judged according to the ‘law of liberty’ naturally raises the question, at least in the minds of some Christians, ‘What judgment? - we thought that we were saved by faith and that we did not have to worry about the judgment.’ And so James makes clear just what kind of faith it is that will provide security in the judgment.”  
**Locus:** R3 L26; Jas 2:12–14

### C-R3-010 — Broader context: capstone of “true religion” begun at 1:21
**Claim:** For Moo, 2:14–26 is the capstone of James’s presentation of “true religion” begun in 1:21: “true religion” begins with faith—but a faith that works; the faith vs. works antithesis corresponds almost exactly to hearing/doing the word in 1:22.  
**Quote:** “For this paragraph is the capstone on James’s presentation of ‘true religion,’ begun in 1:21. … ‘true religion’ begins with faith - but a faith that works. In this sense the ‘true religion’ of 1:26 is nothing more than the genuine faith of 2:14-26, and the faith vs. works antithesis of this paragraph corresponds almost exactly to the ‘hearing the word’/‘doing the word’ antithesis of 1:22.”  
**Locus:** R3 L26–27; Jas 1:21–26; 2:14–26

### C-R3-011 — Against reducing the unit to “generosity only” (vs Davids)
**Claim:** Moo rejects making generosity the primary theme of 2:14–26 (e.g. Davids’s “Generosity Is Necessary”); that unfairly diminishes the broader “true religion” connection.  
**Quote:** “Some commentators, indeed, emphasize this dimension of the paragraph to the extent that they make it the primary theme; Davids, for instance, titles this section ‘Generosity Is Necessary.’ But doing so unfairly diminishes the third, and broadest, connection that 2:14-26 has to the argument of the letter.”  
**Locus:** R3 L26; Jas 2:14–26

### C-R3-012 — Historical occasion: polemic against a misunderstood “faith alone justifies”
**Claim:** Moo argues James’s diatribe style and v. 24’s criticism of “faith only” suggest opposition to false views among the readers; given mid-40s dating, James likely counters a *misunderstood* form of Paul’s teaching (slogan “faith alone justifies”), not Paul’s authentic view, and not Paul as the “foolish man.”  
**Quote:** “the criticism in v. 24 of a ‘faith only’ view of justification suggests further that these false views have some relationship to the apostle Paul. … The readers of the letter, scattered by persecution into areas near Antioch, have become acquainted with a perverted form of the Pauline viewpoint, with the slogan ‘faith alone justifies’ as its hallmark. James writes, then, to counter this false view of the relationship between faith, works, and salvation.”  
**Locus:** R3 L28–29; Jas 2:18, 20, 24

### C-R3-013 — James and Paul not irreconcilable when contexts are respected
**Claim:** Moo holds that James and Paul, properly interpreted in their own contexts, are not opposed; they appear to conflict because they write from different vantage points against different problems.  
**Quote:** “James and Paul, when properly interpreted in their own contexts, are not opposed to one another on this point. They give the appearance of a conflict because they are writing from very different vantage points in order to combat very different problems.”  
**Locus:** R3 L29; intro to 2:14–26

### C-R3-014 — Asyndeton and “my brothers” signal topic shift (v. 14)
**Claim:** Moo notes v. 14 is formally unconnected (asyndeton); “my brothers” suggests a topic shift announced in two related rhetorical questions.  
**Quote:** “Verse 14 is formally unconnected to its context (grammarians call this ‘asyndeton’); and the direct address ‘my brothers’ … suggests a topic shift. James announces the new topic in two related rhetorical questions”  
**Locus:** R3 L41; Jas 2:14

### C-R3-015 — “Claim” (says) already questions the reality of the faith
**Claim:** Moo stresses that the verb “claim” (lit. “says”) suggests from the outset that James questions the reality of the professed faith; the “if” is formally hypothetical but vv. 20ff. show the situation is more than hypothetical.  
**Quote:** “The use of the verb claim (lit. ‘says’) suggests at the outset that James questions the reality of the faith. … Verses 20 and following make clear that the situation is far more than hypothetical.”  
**Locus:** R3 L41; Jas 2:14

### C-R3-016 — erga: general ethical-religious “works,” not Paul’s “works of the law”
**Claim:** Moo defines James’s *erga* as actions done in obedience to God in a general sense; modern versions prefer “deeds/actions” lest “works” carry a negative Pauline connotation (e.g. Eph 2:9). Paul’s “works of the law” echoes Jewish torah-obedience emphasis; James does not use that restricted phrase.  
**Quote:** “James uses ‘works’ in a general sense to refer to actions done in obedience to God. … Paul’s phrase ‘works of the law’ (Gal. 2:16; 3:2, 5, 10; Rom. 3:20, 28) clearly echoes this Jewish emphasis.”  
**Locus:** R3 L42–43; Jas 2:14; cross-ref Paul

### C-R3-017 — “Can such faith save?” expects “no”; anaphoric article = that claimed faith
**Claim:** Moo: the second question (particle *mē*) expects “no”—“That kind of faith can’t save anyone.” The Greek article with “faith” is anaphoric, referring back to the claimed faith of the man without works; James is not denying that the right kind of faith saves.  
**Quote:** “James’s second rhetorical question is put in a form showing that it expects the answer ‘no’ … What James is contesting, then, is that the particular faith he has just mentioned can save. … James’s main point is that this ‘faith’ is, in biblical terms, no faith at all.”  
**Locus:** R3 L44–45; Jas 2:14

### C-R3-018 — Rejection of non-eschatological “save” (earthly rescue only)
**Claim:** Moo rejects the evangelical move that *sōzō* here means only rescue from earthly danger/trial (appealing to 5:14). Elsewhere in James (esp. 1:21 “salvation of souls”) and in the judgment/justification context (2:12–13, 21–25), and in NT epistles generally, “save” has full eschatological force.  
**Quote:** “They avoid the potential difficulty by insisting that the word ‘save’ does not refer here to eschatological deliverance, but to some kind of rescue from earthly danger or trial. … Especially important is the occurrence in 1:21, since the present discussion is part of the argument begun in that verse; and 1:21 speaks definitively about the ‘salvation of souls.’ … Clearly, we must give the verb the full theological force that it normally has in the NT epistles”  
**Locus:** R3 L46; Jas 2:14; 1:21; 5:14; 4:12; 5:20

### C-R3-019 — Movement from general “benefit” to particular saving power
**Claim:** Moo maps the passage: vv. 15–17 elaborate lack of general “benefit” of faith without works; after transition vv. 18–19, James attacks specifically the lack of saving power (using “justify”) in dead faith.  
**Quote:** “in vv. 15-17, he elaborates on the lack of ‘benefit’ generally that one gains from faith without works. Then, after the transition in vv. 18-19, he attacks specifically the lack of saving power (using ‘justify’) in the ‘dead’ faith that produces no works.”  
**Locus:** R3 L48–49; Jas 2:15–25

### C-R3-020 — Illustration: pious words without concrete aid for the poor (vv. 15–16)
**Claim:** Moo reads vv. 15–16 as a (likely hypothetical but typical) church illustration: a inadequately clothed, habitually underfed brother/sister receives a blessing (“go in peace… keep warm and well fed”) without material help; “What good is it?” frames the unit and alludes also to the spiritual state of the inactive “believer.”  
**Quote:** “Faced with an obvious and immediate need, the community member (one of you) responds with pious words but without giving any concrete aid. … ‘It is not the form of the statement that is reprehensible, but its functioning as a religious cover for the failure to act.’”  
**Locus:** R3 L50–55 (Moo citing Johnson on “go in peace”); Jas 2:15–16

### C-R3-021 — Possible allusion to Matthean Sheep and Goats (Matt 25:42–43)
**Claim:** Moo suggests James may allude to Jesus’ teaching that entrance into the kingdom is related to works of charity for the destitute (Matt 25:42–43).  
**Quote:** “James may also make allusion here to the teaching of Jesus in the Matthean parable of the ‘Sheep and the Goats.’ God, says Jesus, will grant entrance into the kingdom on the basis of works of charity, but dismiss from his presence those who fail to relieve the needs of the destitute.”  
**Locus:** R3 L55; Jas 2:15–16; Matt 25:42–43

### C-R3-022 — Dual function of the illustration: poverty ethics + analogy of useless profession
**Claim:** Moo: vv. 15–16 both exemplify unconcern for the poor *and* analogize that empty well-wishing is as useless as profession of faith without deeds.  
**Quote:** “the words of an uncaring believer who fails to act to help a person in need are as useless as the profession of faith of a believer who does not have deeds.”  
**Locus:** R3 L56; Jas 2:15–17

### C-R3-023 — *kath’ heautēn*: faith “in itself” inwardly dead, not merely “alone”
**Claim:** Moo prefers “in itself” over “alone” for *kath’ heautēn*: the faith is not merely outwardly inoperative but inwardly dead—through inherent defect inert (*nekros*). James is not contrasting faith and works as alternative approaches to God, but defective faith vs. genuine faith that results in action.  
**Quote:** “a more likely sense of this phrase is not so much ‘by itself’ as ‘in itself.’ James, in other words, is arguing that the kind of faith he has just described is ‘not merely outwardly inoperative but inwardly dead.’ … He is, rather, contrasting a faith that, because it is inherently defective, produces no works and a faith that, because it is genuine, does result in action.”  
**Locus:** R3 L56–57; Jas 2:17

### C-R3-024 — Objector dialogue (2:18): Dibelius-level difficulty; punctuation undecidable from MSS
**Claim:** Moo (with Dibelius) treats 2:18–19 as among the most difficult NT passages: Greek MSS generally lack punctuation; every solution has difficulties; one must accept the option with fewest difficulties.  
**Quote:** “Martin Dibelius … claims that vv. 18-19 is ‘one of the most difficult New Testament passages in general.’ … We will have to rest content with accepting the interpretation that has the fewest difficulties.”  
**Locus:** R3 L58–59; Jas 2:18–19

### C-R3-025 — Rejected: objector as James’s “ally” (view 1)
**Claim:** Moo rejects reading the speaker as an ally who shares James’s insistence on works: *alla* and diatribe convention mark disagreement; “someone” parallels v. 14’s disagreeable figure and the “you” of v. 20 (“O foolish man”).  
**Quote:** “it does not give a very natural interpretation to the introductory quotation formula, ‘But someone will say.’ The strong adversative ‘but’ (Gk. alla) suggests that the view that James is about to quote is in disagreement with his own.”  
**Locus:** R3 L60–61; Jas 2:18

### C-R3-026 — Rejected: objector attacks James’s faith (views 2a–c, including Hodges textual variant)
**Claim:** Moo rejects forms where the objector doubts James’s faith (strained *kagō*; objector ends up claiming works-demonstration like James; Hodges’s Byzantine variant requires unconvincing irony and rests on a dubious text).  
**Quote:** “However, quite apart from its dubious textual basis the irony necessary to sustain this view is simply not evident.”  
**Locus:** R3 L62–69; Jas 2:18–19

### C-R3-027 — Preferred punctuation: quote = “You have faith; I have deeds” with generalized pronouns
**Claim:** Moo prefers confining the objector’s words to “You have faith; I have deeds,” with “you/I” as general markers of two positions: one person has faith, another works—faith and works as separable entities/gifts (perhaps appealing to Spirit-distributed gifts, 1 Cor 12).  
**Quote:** “the pronouns are not intended to identify James and the opponent specifically. Rather, they are used more generally to distinguish two different people, or two different positions: ‘One person has faith; another has works’ … The objector’s point would be that faith and works are separate entities; separate ‘gifts’ even.”  
**Locus:** R3 L70–72; Jas 2:18a

### C-R3-028 — James’s reply: faith and works inseparable; only works prove genuine saving faith
**Claim:** On Moo’s view, James answers (vv. 18b–19) that faith and works are not optional gifts; only where works are seen is genuine saving faith present. “Show” (*deiknymi*) may mean “prove/demonstrate,” not merely “make visible.”  
**Quote:** “Only where works are seen is genuine, saving faith present. … James, then, may not be challenging the objector to reveal faith by actions, but to prove that he has faith by what he does”  
**Locus:** R3 L72–75; Jas 2:18b

### C-R3-029 — Demons believe (2:19): orthodoxy without heart-and-life; Shema preferred
**Claim:** Moo: the verbal profession is preferably “God is one” (nearer the Shema, Deut 6:4) than bare monotheism; “Good!” may be sincere or sarcastic, but the problem is that confession does not touch heart and life. Demons are among the most “orthodox” of theologians yet *shudder*—possibly an ironical contrast (at least they react) or a hint of judgment-dread for those whose profession lacks works.  
**Quote:** “The demons perfectly illustrate the poverty of verbal profession in and of itself. They are among the most ‘orthodox’ of theologians, James suggests, agreeing wholeheartedly with the Shema … Yet what is their reaction? They shudder. … as demons, knowing something of the true God, yet lacking true faith, shudder in fear of judgment, so also ought people whose verbal profession is not followed up with actions.”  
**Locus:** R3 L76–78; Jas 2:19

### C-R3-030 — “Foolish man” (v. 20): diatribe address, not Paul; *argos* wordplay
**Claim:** Moo: “You foolish man” is typical diatribe address of a fictitious opponent (cf. Rom 2:1; 9:20); “foolish” = “empty,” stubborn hard-hearted ignorance; there is no reason to identify him with Paul. *Argos* (“useless”) = “not-working,” a wordplay on *erga*: faith that does not work does no good, is dead and useless. KJV “dead” in v. 20 rests on an inferior variant.  
**Quote:** “Still less is there any reason to think, as a few radical scholars have suggested, that the ‘foolish man’ is Paul. … Faith that does not ‘work,’ James is saying, ‘does not work’ - it does no ‘good’ (v. 14), is ‘dead’ (vv. 17 and 26) and useless.”  
**Locus:** R3 L80–82; Jas 2:20

### C-R3-031 — Abraham appeal rooted in Jewish tradition (Gen 22; 1 Macc 2:51–52)
**Claim:** Moo: appeal to Abraham as “our father” and to the Aqedah (Gen 22) is natural for Jewish Christians; Philo and especially 1 Macc 2:51–52 (deeds, testing, Gen 15:6 “reckoned”) show the traditional matrix James uses—but James critically introduces faith as the ultimate cause of the works through which Abraham was justified.  
**Quote:** “James’s argument here, then, takes its origin from a widespread Jewish tradition. But vv. 22-23 show that James qualifies the tradition in a critical manner: he introduces faith as the ultimate cause of the works through which Abraham was justified.”  
**Locus:** R3 L83–87; Jas 2:21–23; Gen 22; 1 Macc 2:51–52

### C-R3-032 — v. 21: Abraham’s deeds as instrument (*ex*) of being “justified”—tension with Paul stated
**Claim:** Moo acknowledges the famous tension: James makes Abraham’s *erga* a cause/instrument of justification, while Paul cites Gen 15:6 for faith credited as righteousness and insists justification by faith not by works (e.g. Rom 3:28). Resolution requires careful sense of *dikaioō* and of the Gen 22 participle.  
**Quote:** “in v. 21 James makes Abraham’s ‘deeds’ (erga …) a cause or instrument (ex …) of his being ‘justified.’ Thus arises the famous tension between James and Paul, who appears to contradict James on two key points.”  
**Locus:** R3 L88–89; Jas 2:21; Rom 3:28; Gal 3:6; Rom 4

### C-R3-033 — Pauline *dikaioō* (for comparison): initial forensic verdict by faith
**Claim:** Moo states the Pauline sense many Christians assume: *dikaioō* as God’s initial judicial verdict of “innocence” over the sinner who trusts Christ—but James, writing before Paul, should not be assumed to use the word the same way.  
**Quote:** “Paul uses ‘justify’ (Gk. dikaioo) to denote God’s initial judicial verdict of ‘innocence’ pronounced over the sinner who trusts Jesus Christ in faith. But we must not assume that James, writing before Paul, uses the word in the same way.”  
**Locus:** R3 L90; method for Jas 2:21–24

### C-R3-034 — First sense of *dikaioō* for James: vindicate in the (final) judgment
**Claim:** Moo’s preferred first sense, from LXX legal usage, Judaism, and Matthew (esp. 12:37): *dikaioō* = “vindicate in the judgment,” a verdict based on actual conduct. On this reading Paul = how one *gets into* relationship with God; James = what that relationship must ultimately *look like* for final approval.  
**Quote:** “First, dikaioo might mean ‘vindicate in the judgment.’ … So ‘justify’ in Paul refers to how a person gets into relationship with God, while in James it connotes what that relationship must ultimately look like to receive God’s final approval.”  
**Locus:** R3 L91–95; Jas 2:21; LXX; Matt 12:37

### C-R3-035 — Second sense: “demonstrate to be right” — and Moo’s rejection of it as primary
**Claim:** Moo considers the rarer sense “show to be righteous / vindicate” (cf. Matt 11:19)—on which Abraham’s prior faith-righteousness (Gen 15:6) would be *demonstrated* by deeds. Harmony with Paul would then be easy, but Moo *rejects* this as most likely: rare use; context concerns salvation at judgment (1:21–27; 2:12–14), not mere demonstration; even “show” in v. 18 is more “prove” than “reveal.”  
**Quote:** “Harmony with Paul is quite clear if this second meaning is adopted. But we question whether it is the most likely. Not only is ‘show to be right’ a fairly rare use of the verb, but the meaning does not fit the context as well. … Tentatively, then, we adopt the former meaning of the verb, according to which James is asserting that Abraham was granted a positive verdict in the judgment by God on the basis of his pious acts.”  
**Locus:** R3 L97–100; Jas 2:18, 21; rejection of “demonstrate only” evangelical escape

### C-R3-036 — Gen 22 participle: not necessarily “when” = justification *at* the Aqedah
**Claim:** Moo notes NIV’s “when he offered” has no direct Greek equivalent; the participle may mean “having offered” (verdict after) or, more likely, specify one of Abraham’s deeds (REB: justified *by* his action *in* offering Isaac)—easing the clash with final-judgment sense of *dikaioō*.  
**Quote:** “the word ‘when’ in the NIV has nothing directly corresponding to it in the Greek text … Another possibility, perhaps more likely, is to take the participle as specifying one of the ‘deeds’ of Abraham; see the REV: ‘Was it not by his action, in offering his son Isaac on the altar, that our father Abraham was justified?’”  
**Locus:** R3 L101; Jas 2:21; Gen 22

### C-R3-037 — Faith and works “working together” (*synērgei*); continuous imperfect
**Claim:** Moo: v. 22 presupposes Abraham’s faith throughout; *synērgei* means “work with,” not primarily “assist/produce”; imperfect stresses continuous active faith cooperating with deeds toward justification (from vv. 21, 23), not mere mental reorientation or occasional profession.  
**Quote:** “James’s point is not so much that Abraham’s faith produced his works as that his faith and works cooperated together. … He therefore emphasizes that Abraham’s faith was not confined to a mental reorientation at the time of his ‘conversion’ or to an occasional verbal profession but that it was an active force, constantly at work along with his deeds.”  
**Locus:** R3 L102–107; Jas 2:22

### C-R3-038 — Works “complete” (*teleioō*) faith: reach intended goal, not repair a faulty faith
**Claim:** Moo rejects Calvin’s idea that works merely *revealed* faith as perfect; *teleioō* = complete/bring to maturity. Parallel to 1 John 4:12: as God’s love is “made complete” when it reaches its goal in our love, so Abraham’s faith reached its intended goal when he obeyed—faith is not incomplete in the sense of inadequate until works are bolted on.  
**Quote:** “Clearly our love does not ‘complete’ God’s love in the sense that the love of God is inadequate or faulty without our response. It is rather that God’s love comes to expression, reaches its intended goal, when we respond to his grace with love toward others. So also, Abraham’s faith, James suggests, reached its intended goal when the patriarch did what God was asking him to do.”  
**Locus:** R3 L108–109; Jas 2:22; 1 John 4:12

### C-R3-039 — Gen 15:6 “fulfilled” (*plēroō*): ultimate significance of faith-and-righteousness in a life of obedience
**Claim:** Moo: “fulfill” here is broader than prophecy-fulfillment—“bring to ultimate significance.” Abraham received right-status by faith *before* works/circumcision (Paul’s chronological point); that faith and God’s acquittal were “filled up” when faith was perfected by works; after the Aqedah the angel reasserts the verdict (“now I know that you fear God,” Gen 22:12).  
**Quote:** “What he is suggesting is that Abraham’s faith, in its relationship to righteousness, found its ultimate significance and meaning in Abraham’s life of obedience. When Abraham ‘put faith in’ the Lord, God gave him, then and there, the status of a right relationship with him: before he had done works, before he was circumcised. This is Paul’s point about Abraham (Rom. 4:1-17). But the faith of Abraham and God’s verdict of acquittal were ‘filled up,’ given their ultimate significance, when Abraham ‘perfected’ his faith with works.”  
**Locus:** R3 L110–112; Jas 2:23; Gen 15:6; Gen 22:12; Rom 4

### C-R3-040 — Forensic (not merely moral) “righteousness” in Gen 15:6 for James
**Claim:** Moo rejects Ziesler’s moral reading (“faith-completed-by-works *is* righteousness”); given “justify” in vv. 21, 24, James assumes forensic status of rightness with God. Timing of conferral is not James’s issue—character of the faith that is credited is.  
**Quote:** “In light of word usage and context, then, James probably assumes a forensic meaning for the term, indicating the status of ‘rightness’ that Abraham attained with God. … When that righteousness is conferred is simply not an issue for James here.”  
**Locus:** R3 L113; Jas 2:21–24; Gen 15:6

### C-R3-041 — James and Paul on Gen 15:6: different biblical-theological settings, not contradiction of basic sense
**Claim:** Moo: without necessarily disagreeing on the verse’s basic sense, Paul seizes chronological placement (initial declaration by faith alone); James treats Gen 15:6 more as a “motto” for Abraham’s life as a whole.  
**Quote:** “Paul seizes on the chronological placement of Gen. 15:6 and cites it as evidence of the initial declaration of righteousness that Abraham attained from God solely on the basis of faith. James views the same verse more as a ‘motto,’ applicable to Abraham’s life as a whole.”  
**Locus:** R3 L114–115; Jas 2:23; Gen 15:6; Rom 4; Gal 3

### C-R3-042 — “Friend of God”: Jewish tradition rooted in OT; antithesis to friendship with the world (4:4)
**Claim:** Moo: “friend of God” is not a direct OT quotation but widespread Jewish tradition (Jubilees, Philo, T. Abraham) with OT roots (2 Chron 20:7; Isa 41:8 “beloved”); it marks privileged status from deep faith and practical obedience—supreme example of friendship with God vs. the world (Jas 4:4).  
**Quote:** “James cites it as an indication of the privileged status Abraham was given on account of his deep faith and practical obedience. He therefore stands for James ‘as the supreme example of what it means to have “friendship with God” rather than “friendship with the world”’ (Jas. 4:4).”  
**Locus:** R3 L116–118; Jas 2:23; 4:4

### C-R3-043 — v. 24 centerpiece: justified by works and not by faith alone
**Claim:** Moo treats v. 24 as the conceptual center of 2:21–25: shift from interlocutor (singular “you see”) to plural readers; programmatic “person” (*anthrōpos*); *dikaioō* = God’s final declaration of innocence at judgment; present tense states timeless truth.  
**Quote:** “This verse is the center of James’s discussion of faith, works, and justification (vv. 21-25). … a person is justified by what he does and not by faith only. … ‘Justify’ will have the same meaning that it did in v. 21: God’s final declaration of a person’s ‘innocence’ before him at the time of the judgment.”  
**Locus:** R3 L120–121; Jas 2:24

### C-R3-044 — “Works of the law” narrowing does not resolve Paul–James for Moo
**Claim:** Moo rejects harmonies that confine Paul’s “works of the law” to ceremonial observances, and also the newer restriction that Paul only excludes *torah-context* works: Rom 3:28 with 4:1–8 shows “works of the law” as a subset of “works”; Rom 3:28 excludes works of any kind from (Pauline) justification.  
**Quote:** “Rom. 3:28, then, excludes works of any kind from justification.”  
**Locus:** R3 L122–126; Rom 3:28; 4:1–8; Jas 2:24

### C-R3-045 — “Faith alone” in James = the bogus faith under attack, not Pauline *pistis*
**Claim:** Moo’s key lexical resolution: “alone” marks the claimed, dead, useless faith of v. 14/17/20/26—not what Paul means by faith. Pauline faith unites the believer to Christ as Lord and includes obedience (“obedience of faith,” Rom 1:5; “faith working through love,” Gal 5:6)—exactly the living faith James propagates. Paul would not quarrel with denying that *that* “faith alone” justifies.  
**Quote:** “The addition of ‘alone’ shows clearly that James refers to the bogus faith that he has been attacking throughout this paragraph: the faith that a person ‘claims’ to have (v. 14); a faith that is, in fact, ‘dead’ (vv. 17 and 26) and ‘useless’ (v. 20). This faith is by no means what Paul means by faith. … Once we understand ‘faith alone,’ then, as a neat summary of the bogus faith that James is criticizing, we can find no reason to expect that Paul would have any quarrel with the claim that ‘faith alone’ does not justify.”  
**Locus:** R3 L127–129; Jas 2:24; Rom 1:5; Gal 5:6

### C-R3-046 — Two-stage justification resolution (Paul initial / James final) + Calvin
**Claim:** Remaining tension (James: works necessary basis/means of justification; Paul: works have no place) is resolved by different referents of *dikaioō*: Paul = initial declaration of the sinner’s innocence by faith; James = ultimate validation at the last judgment that takes into account works true faith inevitably produces. Calvin: Paul contends we are justified apart from works’ help; James does not allow those lacking good works to be reckoned righteous.  
**Quote:** “Paul refers to the initial declaration of a sinner’s innocence before God; James to the ultimate verdict of innocence pronounced over a person at the last judgment. If a sinner can get into relationship with God only by faith (Paul), the ultimate validation of that relationship takes into account the works that true faith must inevitably produce (James). As Calvin puts it, ‘… as Paul contends that we are justified apart from the help of works, so James does not allow those who lack good works to be reckoned righteous.’”  
**Locus:** R3 L130–131; Jas 2:21, 24; Paul on justification

### C-R3-047 — Rahab (v. 25): parallel to Abraham; *dikaioō* again = vindicate in judgment
**Claim:** Moo: v. 25 parallels v. 21 formally (even a prostitute justified for what she did); “when” again exemplifies the works; *dikaioō* again = vindicate in judgment. Rahab (Josh 2) hid and sent off the spies; James calls her *pornē* and the spies *angeloi* (messengers). Faith is inferred from OT and the Abraham parallel though not named.  
**Quote:** “Considered righteous, or ‘justify’ (dikaioo), will again mean ‘vindicate in the judgment’ … While James does not specifically mention Rahab’s ‘faith,’ it can certainly be inferred both from the OT itself and from the parallel with Abraham.”  
**Locus:** R3 L132–146; Jas 2:25; Josh 2

### C-R3-048 — Why Rahab? Variety / anyone can act on faith (not only proselyte or hospitality traditions)
**Claim:** Moo finds proselyte typology and 1 Clement faith-and-hospitality tradition only partly helpful; simplest sufficient answer: variety—beside the celebrated male “friend of God,” an obscure Gentile woman of low moral character implies anyone can act on faith. Possible contrast with the dead faith of the unhelpful “believer” in 2:15–16.  
**Quote:** “So alongside the famous and celebrated ancestor of the Jewish people, a man, ‘the friend of God,’ he places an obscure Gentile woman of low moral character. Thus he implies that anyone is capable of acting on his or her faith - whether a patriarch or a prostitute.”  
**Locus:** R3 L147–151; Jas 2:25

### C-R3-049 — Body without spirit (v. 26): general analogy; reject Hodges’s body=faith inversion
**Claim:** Moo: spirit = life principle that animates the body; without it the body ceases to be—so faith without deeds ceases to be biblical faith, becoming mere profession. Frame with v. 20 around the dialogue. Rejects Zane Hodges’s over-reading that works invigorate faith as the spirit invigorates the body. Again: not works *added* to faith, but possession of a “faith that works.”  
**Quote:** “without the spirit the body ceases to be. In the same way, James suggests, faith that is not accompanied by works ceases to be. It becomes mere profession and has no claim to be biblical faith. We again emphasize that James is not arguing that works be ‘added’ to faith, but that one possess the right kind of faith, a ‘faith that works.’”  
**Locus:** R3 L152–155; Jas 2:26

### C-R3-050 — Luther on living, busy, active faith (preface to Romans)
**Claim:** Moo closes by citing Luther (ironically, given Luther’s famous tension with James) as capturing 2:14–26 forcefully: faith is a living, busy, active, mighty thing that inevitably does good works; whoever does not do such works is an unbeliever who talks about faith and works without knowing either.  
**Quote:** “O it is a living, busy active mighty thing, this faith. It is impossible for it not to be doing good things incessantly. … Whoever does not do such works, however, is an unbeliever. He gropes and looks around for faith and good works, but knows neither what faith is nor what good works are. Yet he talks and talks, with many words, about faith and good works.”  
**Locus:** R3 L156–157; Moo citing Luther, preface to Romans; on Jas 2:14–26

### C-R3-051 — Diatribe device: imaginary interlocutor for instruction
**Claim:** Moo places the objector within ancient diatribe style (cf. Paul in Romans and 1 Cor 15:35): an imaginary interlocutor poses objections so the author can instruct readers; the person is not simply an “ally.”  
**Quote:** “A key component of the diatribe style was the frequent quotation of an imaginary interlocutor to advance one’s own argument. … But 1 Cor. 15:35 is the closest parallel to Jas. 2:18.”  
**Locus:** R3 L14, L61; Jas 2:18; 1 Cor 15:35

### C-R3-052 — Mitton on accurate theology that must “possess us”
**Claim:** Moo cites Mitton approvingly on 2:19: accurate theology is good only if it also possesses us—applied especially to professional theologians, with a C. S. Lewis anecdote about constant contact with “holy things.”  
**Quote:** “As Mitton puts it, ‘It is a good thing to possess an accurate theology, but it is unsatisfactory unless that good theology also possesses us.’”  
**Locus:** R3 L76; Jas 2:19

### C-R3-053 — Still apparent contradiction only if same sense of justify assumed
**Claim:** Moo’s integration thesis: monergistic entry by faith (Paul) is compatible with final validation by the works that Spirit/implanted-word-generated true faith inevitably produces (James); the problem is spurious “faith only” slogans and the “demonstrate only” soft-pedaling of James’s soteriological *sōzō*/*dikaioō*.  
**Quote:** “Trying to add works to a bogus faith is an exercise in futility, for only by ‘accepting the implanted word’ (1:21) and experiencing the inner transformation that it brings can one produce works pleasing to God. … If a sinner can get into relationship with God only by faith (Paul), the ultimate validation of that relationship takes into account the works that true faith must inevitably produce (James).”  
**Locus:** R3 L24, L130–131; Jas 1:21; 2:14–26
